nameStory: The Spotfin Killifish gets its name from the distinctive dark spot, called an ocellus, that decorates the back fin of adult males like a bold eye-spot. This circular marking makes them easy to distinguish from their close relatives when you can get a good look at their fins.
description: The Spotfin Killifish is a tiny, hardy fish that's perfectly adapted to life in the harsh salt marsh environment. These small survivors rarely grow longer than 2 inches, spending their entire lives in shallow tidal pools, puddles, and narrow channels that regularly flood and dry out. They have a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body typical of their killifish family, with a slightly flattened head and large eyes positioned to watch for danger from above.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny fish rarely exceeding 2 inches long - you could easily hold one in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Adult males display a distinctive dark circular spot (ocellus) on the back edge of their dorsal fin, like a painted eye; the dorsal fin sits farther back on the body than in similar species

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined and torpedo-shaped with a slightly flattened head, built for quick movements in shallow water

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Variable coloring that closely resembles the Mummichog, typically olive-brown to gray with darker vertical bars along the sides

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in salt marsh pools, shallow tidal channels, and temporary puddles that smell strongly of salt and decay

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Count only 8-9 rays in the dorsal fin (versus 11-12 in the similar Mummichog)

habitat: This specialized fish lives exclusively in New England's salt marshes, particularly in shallow pools, temporary puddles, and narrow tidal channels that flood and drain with the tides. You'll find them in the upper reaches of salt marshes where the water is often warmer and saltier than the main channels, surviving in conditions that would stress most other fish species. They thrive in areas with muddy bottoms rich in organic matter, often among salt marsh grasses and cordgrass.

seasonality.spring: Spawning activity begins as water temperatures warm, with males developing their brightest fin spots and most intense coloration for attracting mates.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily observed in warm, shallow pools; males display prominent fin spots during breeding season.
seasonality.fall: Still active but preparing for winter by seeking deeper pools within the marsh system that are less likely to freeze completely.
seasonality.winter: Become sluggish and may survive in ice-covered pools by slowing their metabolism dramatically, though they remain more active than many other fish species.

funFact: Spotfin Killifish are true survivors that can live in water so salty it would kill most other fish, and they can even survive being temporarily stranded in drying mud puddles by burrowing slightly and waiting for the next high tide to rescue them.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Mummichog, which shares the same salt marsh habitat and similar coloring. Remember: Spotfin males have that distinctive dark spot on their back fin (like a painted bullseye), while Mummichogs lack this marking and have more dorsal fin rays when you count them carefully.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'killifish,' this species doesn't kill other fish - the name comes from the Dutch word 'kil' meaning small stream or channel, referring to their preferred shallow water habitats.
compareHints: Among its Fundulus relatives, the Spotfin Killifish is distinguished by its male's prominent fin spot and fewer dorsal fin rays compared to Mummichogs, while being much smaller and more salt-tolerant than the freshwater Banded Killifish. Unlike the larger Striped Killifish that moves between salt and fresh water, Spotfins spend their entire lives in the saltiest parts of the marsh.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mummichogs are much chunkier and more robust than their relatives the striped killifish and banded killifish, which have more elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies.
Unlike the irregular dark bars of the mummichog, striped killifish display organized, straight stripes.
Unlike its saltwater cousin the mummichog, which has a more mottled, camouflaged appearance, the banded killifish sports clean, crisp vertical stripes and sticks to freshwater.
